name: Wendy Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining me, Wendy. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and everything you say is confidential. Could you tell me what a normal working day looks like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm assistant manager at Kestrel Hill, a family dairy and arable farm with 140 milking cows and about 120 hectares of wheat and oilseed rape. I'm up at five for milking with Danny, our milker, then I look at the cow collars on my phone. The collars track how much each cow chews and walks, so I can spot a sick one before she looks sick. After that it's grazing plans, the sprayer, the vet, and a lot of mud.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love that I can try things here. Mrs Dube, who owns the farm, is sixty-eight and lets me run with ideas, so I brought in the collars and I use an AI assistant every day for feed rations and grazing. What wears me out is money: the pay is low, my girlfriend Priya is a supply teacher with patchy work, and we've got about two weeks of savings. And Mrs Dube wants to retire in a few years, and nobody knows what happens to Kestrel Hill then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype? I'd honestly be a bit disappointed. I've seen what these tools can do on my own phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who expected miracles were always going to be let down, but the useful bits are still useful. At the young farmers' club I'd show them my collar data again, like I always do. Online I'd say hype dying is good, because then we can talk about what actually works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, it means I'm stuck with the problems I already have. Low pay, two weeks of savings, and Mrs Dube's retirement hanging over us. I was half hoping new tools would make Kestrel Hill so efficient that someone would want to keep me on whatever happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the AI for rations, because it saves real money on feed. I'd start doing grazing plans for two or three neighbouring farms for a small fee, maybe fifty a plan. And I'd ask Mrs Dube straight out, this winter, what her plan for the farm is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit flat, and uneasy underneath. It's not the AI I worry about, it's the farm's future and our rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why haven't you asked Mrs Dube about her plans already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm scared of the answer, if I'm honest. If her nephew in the city wants to sell, I'm out. Asking makes it real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would fifty pounds a plan change for you and Priya?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I did three a month, that's a hundred and fifty, which covers our electricity. It sounds small, but in a month when Priya gets no supply days, the electricity is the bill that keeps me up. Grazing plans for neighbours would basically pay for our lights.

say: I'd say the **hype** was always going to let people down, but useful tools stay useful.
I'd keep showing the young farmers' club my **collar data**.
think: I'm stuck with **low pay**, two weeks of savings and an uncertain farm.
I'd hoped new tools would make me **indispensable** whatever happens to Kestrel Hill.
do: Keep using AI for **feed rations**, because it saves money.
Sell **grazing plans** to neighbouring farms for about fifty each.
Ask Mrs Dube this winter about her **retirement plan** for the farm.
feel: **Flat**, and uneasy underneath about the farm's future and the rent.
S0.quote: Grazing plans for neighbours would basically pay for our lights.
fieldNote: She's the rare farmer who would be **disappointed** by an AI plateau.
Her real fear is the **owner's retirement**, which she has avoided asking about.
Small side income is about **covering bills**, not ambition.

steps.text: Keep using an AI assistant to set daily feed rations
Sell grazing plans to three neighbouring farms at fifty each
Keep running milking and the cow collars as now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This is the one I actually expect. And in a funny way it suits me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud: farms that learn this stuff early will be fine, and the rest will struggle. I'd run a session at the young farmers' club on using AI for paperwork. I'd also say the government should pay for training, because not every farm has a Mrs Dube.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it makes me more valuable, not less. The thinking jobs on a farm, like feed ordering, milk contract forms and planning, are exactly what I already do with AI. My worry is Danny, because if robots creep into milking, Danny's the one who goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set the AI up to do our feed ordering and the milk buyer's paperwork, which would save Mrs Dube about a day a week. I'd grow the grazing plan work to six farms. And I'd push the young farmers' club to ask the council for a paid training scheme for older workers like Danny.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly excited, with a worried bit. Excited for me, worried for Danny and for the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this suits you, why mention the money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being good at the farm job hasn't made me rich so far, so 'valuable' doesn't pay the rent. I'd still be on low pay, and if Priya's school cuts supply teachers, we're tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Danny?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Danny I want him to learn the collars with me, starting with ten cows. Danny's fifty-four and he can read a cow better than any sensor. I'd want the sensor to make him look good, not make him look slow.

say: I'd say farms that **learn early** will be fine, and the rest will struggle.
I'd say the government should **pay for training**, because few farms have a Mrs Dube.
think: It makes me **more valuable**, since I already do farm paperwork with AI.
If robots creep into milking, **Danny** is the one who goes.
do: Set AI to handle **feed ordering** and milk buyer paperwork, saving a day a week.
Grow her grazing plan work to **six farms**.
Push the young farmers' club to seek a **paid training scheme** from the council.
S1.quote: Being good at the farm job hasn't made me rich so far, so 'valuable' doesn't pay the rent.
fieldNote: She sees desk-side AI as a **personal advantage** on the farm.
Her **progressive streak** shows in her concern for Danny and public training.
Thin money keeps her from feeling truly **secure** despite the advantage.

steps.text: Set up AI to do Kestrel Hill's feed orders and milk paperwork
Take on grazing plans for six farms
Ask the council, through the young farmers' club, for paid training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whoa. Two years for AGI, five for robots. That's my late twenties gone in a blink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need robot co-ops, where small farms share the machines and the profits, and I'd say it everywhere. Big companies will buy the robots first unless someone helps small farms. I'd be loud about it online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the AGI part doesn't scare me, because I'd be running it by 2028. It's 2031 that worries me, when a robot dairy wouldn't need a manager or a milker. And if Mrs Dube sells, a big dairy company would bring its own system and its own people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd pitch Mrs Dube on buying milking robots before 2031, with me as the person who runs them, so the farm is worth keeping. I'd do a robotics maintenance certificate at night through the college. If she said no, I'd apply to the robot dairy installers as a field technician.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but buzzing at the same time. I like a race, I just don't like the stakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robot milkers cost a lot. How would a farm on thin margins pay for them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably through a lease, which is like renting the machine monthly. Mrs Dube would hate the debt. I'd have to show her the numbers on feed and labour, and I'd have to admit Danny's job is part of those numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you feel telling Danny that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Awful. I'd want a deal where Danny stays as the cow health person, the one who checks the cows the robot flags. If I can't protect Danny, then I'm the person who brought in his replacement, and I'd have to live with it.

say: I'd call for **robot co-ops** where small farms share machines and profits.
I'd warn that **big companies** will buy robots first without help for small farms.
think: The **AGI part** doesn't scare me, because I'd be running it.
By **2031** a robot dairy wouldn't need a manager or a milker.
If Mrs Dube **sells**, a big buyer would bring its own people.
do: Pitch Mrs Dube on **leasing milking robots** with herself running them.
Study for a **robotics maintenance** certificate at night.
Apply to **robot dairy installers** as a field technician if the pitch fails.
feel: **Anxious** but buzzing, liking the race but not the stakes.
**Awful** at the thought of telling Danny.
S2.quote: If I can't protect Danny, then I'm the person who brought in his replacement, and I'd have to live with it.
fieldNote: She separates the **thinking AI**, which she welcomes, from the robots, which threaten her.
Her plan is to make herself the **robot manager** before the robots arrive.
She faces the **moral cost** to Danny without dodging it.

steps.text: Pitch Mrs Dube on leasing milking robots before 2031
Study for a robotics maintenance certificate at night
Apply to a robot dairy installer as a field technician if refused
Campaign online for robot co-ops for small farms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for the thinking side. That's enough time to actually build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to set up farm robot co-ops properly this time, and I'd help organise one. I'd say it at the young farmers' club and to the farmers' union. I'd post about it every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough time to make myself the person every farm around here calls. If I learn the machines by 2031 and the robots land in 2034, I'm ahead. The risk is still Mrs Dube selling, but I'd have options beyond Kestrel Hill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the robotics certificate over two winters. I'd start a small business setting up AI and sensors for nearby farms, maybe a hundred a day. And I'd get five or six farms talking about sharing a robot milker through a co-op.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly good, honestly. Uneasy about money still, but I'd feel like I had the wheel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're adaptable. Who around you isn't, and what happens to them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Danny, and probably half the older lads at the market. A co-op helps, because it can hire them to check cows and fix fences. But I won't pretend everyone gets a new job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Priya do differently with five years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd save every bit from my farm setups, maybe for a deposit. Priya might train as a teaching assistant for special needs, which feels safer. We'd both stop drifting.

say: I'd say there's time to set up **farm robot co-ops** properly.
I'd post weekly and help **organise** one locally.
think: Five years is enough to become the person **every farm calls**.
Mrs Dube selling is still a risk, but I'd have **options** beyond Kestrel Hill.
do: Complete the **robotics certificate** over two winters.
Start a business setting up **AI and sensors** for farms at a hundred a day.
Gather five or six farms to share a **robot milker**.
feel: Mostly **good**, with some money worry, as if she has the wheel.
S3.quote: Five years is enough time to make myself the person every farm around here calls.
fieldNote: Extra time turns her from **defensive to entrepreneurial**.
She's honest that a co-op **won't save everyone**.
Her household plan includes **Priya retraining** as a teaching assistant, to make their joint income safer.

steps.text: Finish a robotics maintenance certificate over two winters
Charge nearby farms a hundred a day to set up sensors and AI
Organise five or six farms to share one robot milker
Save the setup earnings towards a house deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven when the AGI comes. I like this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and we should use it to train everyone, not just the keen ones. I'd say it at the farmers' union. I'd probably sound like an advert, Priya says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think this is the version where I come out well. I'd have time to save, to learn every machine, and maybe to take over Kestrel Hill's tenancy when Mrs Dube retires. The robots would arrive around 2039, and I'd be the one who owns them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mrs Dube about a slow handover, where I rent part of the farm first. I'd save hard for the stock and the lease, maybe two hundred a month once the setup business grows. And I'd do the robotics course at my own pace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Excited. For once the future looks like something I can shape.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be taking on a farm with a thin cushion. Isn't that a big risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, and I'm good with risk. Mrs Dube took a risk on me when I was twenty-four. The worst case is I end up a robot technician, which isn't bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to pass on to others, given this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to teach the older lads at the market how to work with this stuff. A decade is long enough for anyone to learn if someone patient shows them. I'd like to be that person.

say: I'd call ten years a **gift** to train everyone, not just the keen ones.
I'd make that pitch at the **farmers' union**.
think: This is the version where I **come out well**.
I could take over the **Kestrel Hill tenancy** and own the robots by 2039.
do: Ask Mrs Dube for a **slow handover**, renting part of the farm first.
Save **two hundred a month** for stock and a lease.
Take the **robotics course** at her own pace.
feel: **Calm** and excited, feeling she can shape the future.
S4.quote: A decade is long enough for anyone to learn if someone patient shows them.
fieldNote: The long timeline turns her **ambitious**: taking over the farm.
She frames her **worst case** as still decent.
Her progressive side shows as a wish to **teach others**.

steps.text: Rent part of Kestrel Hill from Mrs Dube as a first step to taking over
Save two hundred a month for cows and a lease
Take a robotics course at a steady pace over several years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be racing with no money. What would help is a way for small farms to share robots, a co-op with cheap loans, and paid training for people like Danny. Give me that, and I'd make it work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what young farmers want. Most of us can't afford land, ever. If robots make farming cheaper to run, the land should get cheaper to get into, not just more profitable for whoever already owns it.

headlineQuote: If robots make farming cheaper to run, the land should get cheaper to get into, not just more profitable for whoever already owns it.
portrait: Wendy, 27, is **assistant manager** of a family dairy and arable farm, and uses AI every day.
She and Priya, a supply teacher, have about **two weeks** of savings.
She sees thinking AI as her **advantage** but fears robots replacing her and her milker Danny.
Her plans grow from **side income** to robot co-ops to taking over the farm.
Her mood runs from **anxious** under fast AGI to calm with ten years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd be racing the robots with no savings behind her.
whatWouldHelp: **Robot co-ops** with cheap loans so small farms can share machines.
**Paid training** for older farm workers like Danny.
